title: The Geometry of Quantum Complexity in Open Systems
authors: Ezra Acalapati, Kausik Ghosh, Giuseppe Policastro
abstract: We extend Nielsen's geometric approach for quantum complexity from closed to open quantum systems, whose dynamics is governed by Lindbladian evolution. In this framework, complexity is defined through an optimal-control problem on the space of mixed states, with a cost assigned to both unitary and non-unitary generators. We show that the resulting geometric structure differs fundamentally from the Riemannian geometry that emerges in the case of unitary evolution. In the open-system setting, the natural geometry is typically sub-Finslerian. Dissipation makes the geodesics non-reversible, while the admissible tangent directions are restricted by the physically allowed controls. We analyze several physically motivated examples, including a single qubit subject to depolarizing and amplitude-damping channels, as well as the damped harmonic oscillator. We show that, similarly to the unitary case, varying the penalty factors in the cost functional modifies the geometric properties through changes in the flag curvature, the Finslerian analog of sectional curvature. Our results provide a geometric framework for quantifying the abstract notion of complexity in dissipative quantum systems, with potential connections to experimentally realizable setups.
summary: This paper extends the concept of quantum complexity from ideal closed systems to real-world open systems subject to dissipation. It reformulates complexity as an optimal control problem on the space of mixed states, revealing that the resulting geometry is sub-Finslerian rather than Riemannian. This provides a powerful geometric tool for quantifying information processing limits in noisy quantum devices.
main_problem: The core problem is extending the geometric definition of quantum complexity, originally for closed systems, to open quantum systems governed by dissipation.
main_result: The geometry in open systems is fundamentally sub-Finslerian rather than Riemannian due to irreversible dissipation, providing a new framework to quantify complexity in realistic noisy environments.
method: Complexity is defined via an optimal control problem on the space of mixed states, analyzed using tools from Finsler geometry and incorporating costs for both unitary and non-unitary generators.
model_or_system: The analysis uses open quantum systems described by density matrices evolving under the Lindblad equation. Specific models include a single qubit with depolarizing/amplitude-damping channels and the damped harmonic oscillator.
key_observables: Complexity, flag curvature (Finslerian analog of sectional curvature), and non-reversibility of geodesics.
important_parameters: Penalty factors in the cost functional; dissipation rates ($\Gamma$); Hamiltonian parameters ($H$).
main_assumptions: The dynamics are governed by the Lindblad equation (CPTP maps). The geometry is generally sub-Finslerian because the evolution is constrained by physical dissipation.
paper_structure: The paper builds from the known unitary case to the open system generalization, deriving the necessary optimal control formulation and analyzing how dissipation modifies the underlying geometric structure (Riemannian $	o$ sub-Finslerian).
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the quantification of complexity in realistic, dissipative quantum systems, which is a major frontier connecting quantum information theory with open quantum dynamics.
